rv.q: The production brings a masterful delicacy to Paula Vogel's Pulitzer Prize-winning memory play.
The play itself still sticks in my throat, as it surely does every woman and girl, young or old, who has seen it in a halfway decent production.
The play’s full impact is finally being felt on Broadway, and it’s forceful, direct and too jarring to ignore.
If I could direct a scene representing why I love theater, it would look something like this: Mary

How I Learned to Drive remains incisive and affecting, not only in the ways that it explores sexual trauma as a personal experience but also in how it places that experience within a larger social matrix: the waiters and other enablers who turn blind eyes, the family members who enforce bad rules.
Vogel's emotionally complex masterwork remains as unsettling, disarmingly funny and as deeply moving as ever.
Truly, “How I Learned to Drive” was a groundbreaking play, if you can imagine that adjective being used for the first time.
Strange things happen when nostalgia gets wrapped up in the production, which is itself a cautionary tale about letting atmosphere drug the senses.
Her simultaneous confidence and vulnerability is always worth experiencing, even when the production doesn’t share it.
With an abundant playwright’s sophistication, Vogel has contributed to comprehending the fathomless complexities of human behavior.
So, grab a ticket, buckle up and experience one of the most exhilarating, and yes unsettling, rides of this – or any – theatrical season.
Thanks to the brilliance of its construction and the power of its insights, you can call it, without contradiction, a modern masterpiece.
If you are reading this, you may be about to break this critic’s other recommendation—that you go see it (really, go see it!), without knowing anything about it.
Far from being a casting gimmick, their return to the play has allowed them to imbue their work with far greater complexity.
This is a tale woven with magic thread.
This mesmerizing incarnation of How I Learned to Drive, affirms Paula Vogel’s achievement and showcases its tremendous actors.

There are many reasons why people are skeptical of revivals, especially ones that trot out an original cast member for box office nostalgia's sake. But How I Learned to Drive, finally on America's most visible stage, is neither showy nor superfluous.
How I Learned to Drive is the most challenging, thought-provoking play of the season, and thank God it's finally on Broadway.
Well, any nuance that Vogel missed is provided by Morse’s subtle, masterful performance.

Brokaw’s stripped-down and highly-effective production accentuates the complex relationship between Li’l Bit and Peck, with Parker and Morse (who is impressively understated) giving nothing short of a masterclass in acting.
It’s a valuable reminder, and however familiar the subject matter of How I Learned To Drive may now seem, the play and this production will haunt you.
Another wonder in Brokaw's revisiting of the play is the emphasis on the family which fosters the dangerous liaison.
“How I Learned to Drive” is not just a play about seduction and complicity; it is itself a kind of seduction, which charms us, and then makes us feel complicit.

Mr. Morse, stolidly believable, restrained, and unflashy, is thoroughly convincing as the gently persistent, even kindly, older man with a penchant for young flesh...; he beautifully manages the challenging trick of making Peck, for all his creepiness, almost sympathetic.
Her visceral vulnerability in those scenes of childhood assaults cannot be spared by the retrospective certainty of her survival.
Rather, it reveals the fear of all survivors: that they will never escape the room where they were violated.
While Parker and Morse’s performances and Mark Brokaw’s direction are solid and well-executed, How I Learned to Drive nonetheless falls short of the great theater it may once have been.
It is clear that the focus was on Parker and Morse’s performances, and they so superbly showcase that this play is a masterpiece.

If you consider yourself a true theater lover, you should see it if there is any way that you can get to Manhattan Theatre Club's Samuel J. Friedman Theater before its run there is scheduled to end on May 29.
This is more than just a revival—it’s a reinvigoration of what I consider to be one of the best works of the last 50 years.

cn.t: Critics praise this Pulitzer-winner's long-overdue Broadway debut, with Parker and Morse delivering powerful performances in their original roles. Vogel's complex exploration of abuse remains unsettling yet deeply moving, though some find its nuance harder to embrace post-#MeToo.

sg.ra: SeatPlan notes rows A-D are ideal at this 634-seat house: close enough to catch facial expressions but not neck-craning. Row AA also called out for superior legroom. No overhang concerns (Mezzanine overhang starts at row G per SeatPlan).

Headout and SeatPlan both flag rows E-J as the best price-to-sightline ratio: meaningfully cheaper than the A-D premium band while staying close in a 634-seat room. Slight orchestra rake keeps sightlines clean. Mezzanine overhang (per SeatPlan) begins at row G but the intimate room means no sound-deadening issue in this band.

sg.vl: Under the overhang but still engaged
sg.ra: SeatPlan confirms the Mezzanine overhangs from row G back, so K-Q sit fully under. The room is small enough (Headout: 'one of Broadway's more intimate spaces') that rear orchestra remains engaged. Rows P and Q are accessibility-friendly (no aisle stairs per folliesbroadway). Legroom tightens beyond row O per SeatPlan.

Headout and SeatPlan both name AA-BB center as premier seats with 'clean, direct look at the stage' and elevation that improves the view. aviewfrommyseat user on Mezzanine L row A aisle reported 'lots of legroom' with only a thin safety bar as minor issue. Excellent rake across the mezzanine.

SeatPlan and Headout both emphasize that the mezzanine has 'excellent rake' keeping all rows elevated with clean sightlines; Headout says 'no truly bad seat in the house'.
